claims.text: High configurational entropy stabilizes a chemically disordered, single-phase solid solution in equiatomic multi-element HEAs.
High configurational entropy reduces the thermodynamic driving force for phase separation and precipitation.
Severe lattice distortion arises from atomic-size mismatch in five-component HEA nanoparticles.
Lattice distortion and complex local chemical environments create high activation-energy barriers for atomic diffusion.
Low atomic diffusion kinetically restrains precipitate formation.
Sluggish diffusion inhibits both the nucleation and growth of precipitates.
A single-phase Al0.1CoCrFeNi HEA exhibits phase stability against ion irradiation, with no precipitates observed even at the highest tested fluence.
Nearly equiatomic five-transition-metal HEA nanoparticles will resist precipitation and phase separation at elevated temperatures.
The nanoparticles will retain their nanoscale dimensions during elevated-temperature exposure.
Traditional binary or ternary alloys undergo rapid diffusion, precipitation, phase separation, or coarsening under comparable elevated-temperature conditions.
Multiphase HEAs have lower effective configurational entropy than true multi-element solid solutions because ordering and phase separation reduce configurational entropy.
Multiphase AlxCoCrFeNi HEAs form numerous coherent precipitates under ion irradiation, unlike the single-phase Al0.1 composition.
Some low-Al AlxCrCoFeNi compositions show substantial chemical clustering over a wide temperature range.
At sufficiently small nanoparticle sizes, surface energy can dominate bulk configurational-entropy stabilization.
At sufficiently high temperature, kinetic diffusion barriers can be overcome, permitting coarsening or melting.
The proposed entropy-based stabilization mechanism does not apply if the initial alloy is naturally multiphase and has reduced configurational entropy.
Longitudinal spin fluctuations affect finite-temperature phase stability in CoCrFeMnNi.
The specific contribution of magnetic fluctuations to the stability of CoCrFeMnNi nanoparticles is not established by the cited evidence.

contradictions.description: The boundary permits loss of stability once sufficiently high temperature overcomes kinetic barriers, potentially before melting, whereas the falsification rule treats a transition to a multiphase or ordered state at any temperature below melting as falsifying intrinsic stability. The experiment therefore does not clearly distinguish an admitted high-temperature failure boundary from falsification of the mechanism.
